utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. Yes. You're going to call your client, Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, Your Honour. But I thought that before that, some questions would be raised. But if not, I would like to call Mr. Simo Zaric to take the witness stand before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zaric. Please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, you can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Pisarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we were preparing you for your testimony, we were speaking about the technical details of your testimony. That's why I'm not going to give you any particular instructions. However, I would like to ask you that if you find yourself in a situation that you don't hear something or that something doesn't function, please let me know and then we will repeat the question and we will resolve the issue. Mr. Zaric, tell us, please, for the record, your name, your first name and your last name.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: My name is Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Solaja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the meaning of that nickname? Who were you nicknamed after?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I got this nickname -- I was nicknamed after a war hero [Realtime transcript read in error "herey'] from the Second World War, Simela Solaja from the area of Kozara. They called me Simela as a term of endearment. And then I got this nickname, Solaja, which became an integral part of my first and last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your fellow citizens know you by that nickname?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, many of my fellow citizens knew me by that nickname, and the majority of my acquaintances addressed me by that nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction on page 2, line 16. It's a war hero. Here it says "herey."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I was born on 25 July, 1948.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The name of my village is Trnjak Zorice in the area of Odzak municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your native village is called Trnjak Zorice. Can you tell us something about its ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It is of mixed ethnic composition, inhabited by Croats and Muslims -- sorry, Serbs. And I would like to say that there is an equal ratio of Croats and Serbs residing in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where and when did you complete your elementary education?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The first four grades of the elementary school I completed in Zorice, in my native village, and the second part of elementary education I completed in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you attend secondary school, and which school was that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I attended the second school for economics in Bosanski Samac, and it was between 1963 and 1967.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, how long did you reside in Trnjak Zorice village? Up to when?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I resided there up to 1969.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you reside from 1969?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Since 1969, up to this day, save for the five or six years that I spent here in The Hague, I've resided in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you find your first employment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I found my first employment in a state-owned company called Bosanka. It is a trading company where I started to work on the 15th of May, 1969. I stayed there until 15 May, 1975.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What duties did you discharge in that trading company called Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I first started as an intern in the sales. I was calculating the prices. And then, in 1973, I obtained my degree from the higher school of economics. I became the financial director of that company and I discharged the duties of the financial director of that trading company for two years before I left the company and joined another company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: When was it that you graduated from the school of economics, and where was that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: First, I graduated from a higher school of economics in 1973, and then I obtained a full degree in economics, and that was on the 18th of December, 1979, from the school of economics in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could just slow down a little bit for the interpreters. When did you become the chief of SUP in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I became the chief of SUP on the 15th of May, 1975.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that post, in the post of the chief of SUP in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Up to the 1st of August, 1979. A little over four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the expiry of that mandate, after the end of your term, where did you continue your professional career after that? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: After the job of the chief of SUP, I applied for the job of the director of the Buducnost company, and I was given that job and I started working on the 1st of August, 1979. Buducnost is a manufacturing company which produces upholstered and other types of furniture, and it had 1.000 employees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That company, Buducnost, was it a part of some system in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a system of companies, of associated companies?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Buducnost was part of -- one of the largest corporations at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the name of that corporation was Sipad and it was based in Sarajevo. And let me just tell you that there were 52 manufacturing companies, members of that corporation, and those were furniture companies. Besides that, that company also had forests and it had mills and timber processing companies. It was one of the major companies in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, how long did you remain the director of the Buducnost company?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I stayed there in that job until 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. In 1982.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: And then in 1982, I was appointed the director of the representative office of that company in Belgrade for the area of Serbia and two autonomous provinces, that is, Kosovo and Vojvodina. I stayed in that job in Belgrade and I mostly engaged in the sale of furniture produced in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the marketplace where I operated was Serbia, with its two autonomous provinces, Kosovo and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. Again, can you please slow down in giving your answers. How long did you stay in that job, in the job of the representative of the Sipad corporation in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I stayed in that job until the 31st of January, 1985. Then I returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina for family reasons, and from 31st January 1985, I started working in the sector of the State Security Centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please just answer my questions and we will answer other questions at a later stage. While you were in Belgrade, where was your family residing at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: While I was working in Belgrade, my family resided in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you visit your family? How often did you go home?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Every weekend I would take the business train to see my family. There would hardly be a weekend when I didn't go to Bosanski Samac. And sometimes I would also visit my family when business took me to Bosnia and Herzegovina, when I paid visits to the furniture companies whose products I sold on the marketplace in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little while ago you mentioned that you left the job in Belgrade for family reasons. What family reasons were those? Why did you return from Belgrade to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: In January 1982, my father, Mirko, had a stroke. He became severely ill, and that was the only reason for which I returned. I wanted to help my mother look after him. My sisters were all married and they could not dedicate so much time to my father. And I, as his only son, decided to do that. I had a lot of emotional reasons to help my father. Unfortunately, my father lived like that for eight years. But I never regret going back home. Although, if that had not happened, my life would have looked differently and I would have never ended up in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did your mother and father reside? Did they have some property there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: My mother and father resided in Trnjak. We had one of the best farms in that village. And when I say one of the best, then I would like to say that this farm was so well known because we had one of the largest orchards in that area. We had over 300 trees of different fruit. And every time when I had time, I would go there to help them work on that farm. So they indeed reside on a farm in Trnjak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they farmers then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned from Belgrade, where did you find employment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Belgrade, my first job was in Doboj. I worked in the sector of the State Security Centre for a year. I was an inspector. That sector of the state security centre was linked to the Security Services Centre in Doboj and its Superior Command was the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were working in Doboj, did you also reside in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. While I worked in Doboj, I had a temporary residence there, and every weekend I would go back to the area of Samac. I would go back to my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, after a certain period of time, was a detachment of the State Security Centre established in the town of Modrica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The detachment of the State Security Centre was established even before I became the chief. But in February 1986, pursuant to the decision of the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Dusko Zgonjanin, I was transferred and I became the chief of the detachment of the State Security Centre, and this detachment at that time covered the area of three municipalities. Those were the municipalities of Modrica, Bosanski Samac, and Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you move to Modrica with your family?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. My family remained in Samac. I commuted to Modrica every day because the distance between Samac and Modrica is 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, could you explain to the Chamber the structure of the state security at that time and how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The state security service started with the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo. There were two sectors there. One of them was the sector of state security, and the other was the sector of public security. The Ministry of the Interior coordinated the work of both of these services. The chief of the state security was the undersecretary of the state security. So that was the first person in the Ministry of the Interior, reporting directly to the minister and who was in charge of the organisation of that service and who managed that service. The second down the hierarchy were centres for state security, and they were organised in various regions. They also had a similar division. They also had two sectors. One was the state security and the other was the public security sector. The head of the regional centres were chiefs, and each of the respective sectors had their superior. And the third, or the lowest step in that organisational ladder were detachments, and this is precisely where I worked. A detachment would cover some microregions, and there were many more detachments than state security centres. I personally was in the Modrica detachment, which covered three municipalities. There was also a detachment in Derventa, which covered some other municipalities, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. You have explained the structure to us. What were your concrete tasks as the chief of the detachment in Modrica, and what were your authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The state security service is a very specific service. It collects intelligence along various lines of work. When I say that, then I mean that one line of work was collecting intelligence relative to the counter-intelligence of foreign intelligence services in the area of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia, because the state security service was linked up to the service at the federal level. The second line of work was collection of information on the Chetnik Ustasha, and Muslim emigration [Realtime transcript read in error "immigration"] in the diaspora, abroad, not residing in the former Yugoslavia. And the third line of work was collection on intelligence on the activities of the internal forces which jeopardised the constitutional order of the country. The fourth line of work was, for example, the collection of intelligence on significant, vital facilities of particular significance for the state and protection of the most important persons in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia. So those were the lines of work that we carried out, and the task of the state security service was to collect intelligence about all these things, and people were specialised in different types of work:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just clarify something for the transcript? It reads, at line 20 on page 9: "Chetnik, Ustasha, and Muslim immigration in the diaspora." I think it should be emigration, e-m-i-g-r-a-t-i-o-n, rather than immigration. Going out rather than coming in. Perhaps that could be clarified or corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you said emigration, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Correct. Emigration was the word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, as the chief of the detachment in Modrica, if you received some intelligence or if you collected some intelligence, what did you do with that information, with that intelligence? Who did you send reports to about the intelligence that you gathered or obtained?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: In order to gain a clear picture on the size of the detachment, I would like to say that I had five more people working with me in that detachment, and our main task was to collect the so-called initial information at that microregion, and to transform them into the initial official records. I, as the chief of the service, would inspect all those reports. I would certify and sign those reports and I would then forward those reports to the sector in Doboj. As I did that, this completed our operational task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, do you remember, while you were the chief of the detachment, do you remember who your immediate superiors were, both at the regional and the republican level?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Upon arriving in the service, upon joining the service, the republican secretary was Mr. Mato Andric. He was a Croat. And the head, the chief of state security at the time, was Dusko Zgonjanin. In the centre in Doboj, when I arrived there, the chief of the security centre was Bogdan Nikolic, and the chief of the state security sector was Marko Brezanic. Just before I retired, and following the multiparty elections, the entire leadership was changed. So my immediate officer just before I retired in the state security sector in Doboj was Ilija Bilic from the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Alliance. And the chief of the centre was Andrija Bilosevic from the Serbian Democratic Party. He had been appointed as chief so I had, so to speak, two leadership teams. The first one when I arrived there and the second one when I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you just tell us up until which year you worked in the state security service?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Up until the 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, why did you stop working in the SDB, in the state security service?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a long story. I'll try and summarise the basic facts. After the multiparty elections, and when the national and nationalistic parties assumed power, the leaders in the organs of internal affairs were changed. The minister of the interior -- as minister of the interior, Alija Delimustafic was appointed to this post. And as I said earlier on, I've already said what sort of changes occurred in the Doboj centre, which is where my -- which is -- which was my -- the institution that was above me, that I was subordinated to. With a certain number of colleagues in the SDB, in the state security service, I reacted very critically with regard to certain negative appearances that one could notice at the time, and that exerted an influence on the political gulf between the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this complicated the security and political situation. And I wasn't much loved as a leader, given the positions that I held. So on the 1st of October, in the course of the night, I and five of my colleagues of Serbian nationality, and a colleague of Muslim nationality, were retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. When you retired, how old were you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: When I was retired, I was 44 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The fact that you weren't a member of one of the national parties that won the elections, did that have any influence on your premature retirement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: That was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, we will now turn to your family background. Could you tell this Trial Chamber when you married for the first time.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, that part of my curriculum is not the most positive aspect that I could display, but I married in 1969 for the first time, when I came back from the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your wife's nationality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: My first wife was called Milka. She came from a mixed marriage. Her father was a Serb and her mother was a Croat. And I had a daughter, whose name is Natasa, with my wife Milka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After you got divorced from Milka, to whom your daughter Natasa was given for education, she was appointed as her guardian by the court --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's not modest to say so, but at the time, Natasa, who hadn't even started walking at the time, was appointed to me, to the father, as her guardian. I won't go into the reasons. This is a private matter. But what I've said is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, when did you get married for the second time? You don't have to mention the name. Just say what nationality your second wife was.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: In 1972 I got married for the second time. I married a woman who was of Croatian nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any children with that -- with your second wife?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you get married for the third time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It was on the 12th of January, 1974 that I got married for the third time. My third wife's name is Fatima, and she testified before this Tribunal quite recently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Her name is Topcagic, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I had a son, Mirel [Realtime transcript read in error "Miro"] with her, and my wife was married before. And when we got married, she already had a son called Denis. So that Fatima and I fed three children. We had three children to feed. I'm not joking when I say that it was my child and her child, and our child. But in fact these are our lovely children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Zaric. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Page 13, line 22. It's Mirel, the name of Mr. Zaric's son. Nor Miro, it's Mirel, M-I-R-E-L.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've heard this detail before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you still live with Mrs. Fatima, with your third wife; isn't that correct, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, tell us: Since when has your family, Zaric, lived in the Trnjak Zorice village, and when did they arrive in that area?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The Zaric family, I think it's one of the oldest families in that area, they arrived in Trnjak in 1870, from the area of Uzice in Serbia. They arrived in the Posavina area. And from that date to this very day, they live in a village. I'm the only one who is here where I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Could you please tell us now, could you tell this Honourable Trial Chamber: What happened to your family, to the Zaric family, and to other Serbian families, in the area of Trnjak Zorice in December 1944?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the most tragic part of my family's history, without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. I don't understand why we need these details, 1944. I don't think they are relevant to the case. I think we've had enough personal history of Mr. Zaric. Can we proceed with the current issues rather than going back to 1944.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, why did I put this question? Well, above all, because part of this story appears in the interview that Mr. Zaric gave to OTP investigators, and it is for this reason that I thought that it would be reasonable, logical, for Mr. Zaric to tell this Trial Chamber what happened. And secondly, given the nature of the charges levelled against Mr. Zaric, I think that it is of great significance, and it should be, it should be of great significance. It would be significant to know, in addition to the tragedy of the Zaric family, the members of the Zaric family mustered the strength to forgive and to live and to have children with members of other ethnic groups, other nationalities, all the more so given that Mr. Zaric is charged with having committed certain acts on the basis of discrimination. But if the Trial Chamber is aware of these facts, I'm quite prepared to move on to other matters. I just wanted Mr. Zaric to inform us about this briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps very briefly, Mr. Zaric can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you please try to provide us with the main details about that event, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: As I said, that is the most tragic part of my family's story. On the 7th of December, 1944, in the course of the Second World War, 601 Serbs - women, children, old people - they were killed in that village. In the house of my father, Mirko, on that day, 242 people were killed, including two of his sons and three daughters, his mother, his wife, and two sisters, and other relatives, some of his other relatives. One of his sons at the time, his name was Simo -- well, I'm here for biological reasons. His father is -- married my mother and had four children. That was his second marriage. And then he called me after one of his sons who was killed on that day. As far as my mother is concerned, who married my father, she suffered a similar tragic fate as my father did. She lived in Donja Dubica. She got married there. Her husband and her entire family from Klakar, that's a village in the area of the municipality of Brod, they were taken to Jasenovac, where they were all killed. The two of them who remained, who survived, they got married and they had children. And again, there were five children in the Zaric family. I was the only male child, and I have four lovely sisters. The oldest one is Koviljka. She is my half sister. She had the status of a wartime orphan because my mother lost her husband who was taken away to Jasenovac and was killed there. So that would be a very brief outline of that part of my history. But I would just like to say in a very few words that I very seldom -- we very seldom heard about this terrible story from my parents. It was never a subject that was dominant in the Zaric household. And my parents strove to educate us in a new spirit, in a spirit of fraternity and unity. That was a principle for me, and all it meant was that one should live normally with others and be prepared to forgive, whether it's possible to forget such matters, that's another issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, thank you. I would now like to ask you: Who was your half sister, Koviljka, married to, or rather, as you say, your sister, because she grew up on her own. Who was she married to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: My eldest sister, Koviljka, she is married to Mustafa Omeranovic, who is a Muslim. She has three children. She had three children with him, two sons and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is your sister Mara married to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: She is my second elder sister. She is married to Nenad Brocilovic, a Serb, and is currently living in Serbia. And right up until the war, she lived in the area of Odzak, as my other three sisters did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, who is your sister Jelena married to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: My sister Jelena was married to a Muslim. She got divorced before the war and she had one child with him, a son, with whom she lives in Bosanski Samac at the time. He's married and has two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your sister Nada, Dr. Nada, who is she married to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: My younger sister is married to Marko Jakic, a Croat from the village of Osicac which is part of the Odzak municipality. At the moment they live in Kanjiza, in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A minute ago, you said that all your sisters lived in the municipality of Odzak. But where did Koviljka live?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: She lived in Samac, whereas Mara, Jelena and Nada all got married and lived in the municipality of Odzak, or to be more precise in the town of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the fighting broke out, where did your mother Mileva live, your mother Mileva Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: My mother, Mileva Zaric, lived in Trnjak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had a daughter whose name was Natasa tell us who is she married to and where does she live now?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: My daughter Natasa is married to Mario Prgomet. He's a Croat from Bosanski Samac. And up until the war, they lived in the area of Bosanski Samac. But they are now living in Croatia. I have two grandchildren, that is to say, they have two sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Did you perform your military service in the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army? If you did, where and when?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I performed my military service in the JNA from 1967 to 1969. I did my service in three towns in Serbia. First of all, I was in Pozarevac, then Kragujevac and then finally in Sabac. And I was a member of Tito's guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a rank conferred on you while you were performing your military service, and if so, which rank?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a rank, the rank of what we call a "desetar" at the time, nothing else, and that was the rank with which I left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, was another rank conferred on you, that of a non-commissioned officer or an officer?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I was assigned to the reserve police force in the Odzak municipality, because after I had completed my military service I was still living in the territory of Odzak. And in 1969 I moved to Samac and I became a non-commissioned officer. I was a corporal. And when the war broke out, I was a senior corporal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have a rank at the moment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: At the moment I have the rank of first lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, were you ever charged for a crime or misdemeanour of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, never. That never happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now move to your political affiliation. Were you a member of the Communist Party in Yugoslavia; and if so, from which date and until which date?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia since 1966. When I joined the state security service in 1985, they started depoliticising the work of the Ministry of the Interior, so I then ceased with my party activities. And when I retired on the 1st of October, 1991, I joined the Socialist Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was led by Nijaz Durakovic at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the ethnic composition of the SDP in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a civil party. It was recognised as such, above all because members -- people from all ethnic groups were represented in this party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the president of the SDP of Bosnia and Herzegovina was Nijaz Durakovic at that time. Do you remember the names of any other leaders during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I can remember Mr. Lagumdzija at that time. He was a member of the Socialist Democratic Party. And I think that to this very day he is the president of the BH SDP. I can remember Mr. Filipovic. I can remember Dr. Stojanovic and some people -- some other people from that period. But I know that there were people who were members of various ethnic groups, of all the ethnic groups, and they still adhere to the SDP policies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, do you know anything about this matter: What was the position of the BH SDP with regard to the national and religious rights of the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Their position was that they should have total national and religious freedom. People should not be divided according to their nationality, their religion, their race, et cetera. So these were civilian principles, civil principles, which were based on the most modern programmes of democratic parties in Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. In Bosanski Samac municipality, was there a municipal committee of the SDP?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the members of the SDP in the Bosanski Samac municipality were?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know official that the ethnic composition of the SDP in Bosanski Samac at that time -- well, the members were of -- came from various ethnic groups, from all the ethnic groups. But the Serbs were perhaps -- had perhaps the majority, and the Muslims and the Croats to a lesser extent. But I would like to say that people from all the ethnic groups were members of that party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have already heard that the first multiparty elections were held in 1990. There were also elections at the same time for deputies in assembly -- Municipal Assemblies. Do you remember how many deputies the SDP had in the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, during the first multiparty session, during the first multiparty assembly, there were six deputies from the SDP, three from the federation of reformist forces, and I think there were three from Liberal Party, whereas the other deputies in the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac were from the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Could you just tell me whether among the deputies from the SDP, were there Serbs, Croats, and Muslims among their deputies?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember. I know that the deputies at the time -- well, Rajko Kuresevic and Perica Krstanovic and Dr. Sekib, they were deputies at the time. There was someone called Marko Filipovic too. So I know that the ethnic composition of the deputies in the assembly was mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please: Are you now a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since 1993, I've been a member of the Socialist Party of Republika Srpska, and to this very day I am its member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That party, the Socialist Party of Republika Srpska, is it a political successor of the former SDP whose member you were in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: To a large extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You, Mr. Zaric -- let me rephrase that. I'll withdraw that. Was there a municipal board of the Socialist Party in Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was a municipal board, and it played its role in the first multiparty elections after the war, which took place in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that municipal board, did you have some sort of a duty in that municipal board, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the general secretary of the Socialist Party in Samac municipality, and during the first congress of the Socialist Party, I was member of the statutory commission of the Socialist Party of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So much about your political engagement. Let's now move on to some activities and inclinations that you have. And therefore, I would like to ask you about your sports engagement in Samac municipality and in the local commune of Trnjak Zorice.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, that is probably the nicest page of my biography. In that part, I've tried to find myself. I found satisfaction. I was an active athlete. And I also was a member of the cultural society in my village, because I was a good singer. I sang folk songs. I also played football in a number of teams, in the team of Samac, in a number of village teams. I was a good athlete. In 1968, when I served in the JNA, I was a Yugoslav champion in 1500-metre race. As far as my cultural activities are concerned --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Zaric. We will come to your cultural activities, but I would like to talk about sport now. Did you have any role in the sports life apart from you being an athlete?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: When I was younger, I was an active athlete. Later on, when I got a bit older and gained some more authority, then, together with my fellow citizens, I was actively involved from the organisation of sports clubs, in their maintenance. I was a member of many of the management board of sports teams. I was president of a number of clubs. I was the president of the intermunicipal sports alliance in Brcko. Later on, this amateur involvement evolved into something more serious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you stopped playing football, did you appear as a member of a veteran teams? Did you have any activities in that area?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, for eight years, I was an active veteran in the Sloga football club from Prud. That is a Croatian village neighbouring on my village. And that is where I spent most of my football time in the later stages of my life, and that is where I have a lot of friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to your activities within the cultural and artistic life of your community. Can you tell us something about your hobbies, your talents, your activities, and how did all that reflect?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: In the Zaric household, we always fought tragedy with song. Both of my parents were good singers, and I inherited that talent, talent for singing original folk songs that existed in those rural areas. And I would like to say that at that time that song was understood by over 5 million people in the area of the former Yugoslavia. I also recorded my first videocassette of original folk songs with the Begic brothers, who were the best folk singers in the former Yugoslavia. They are Croats who resided in the territory of Derventa. They are still alive and they are still the best singers of those original folk songs. And since I had this talent, I was a member of cultural clubs, and I also appeared on TV show called Knowledge is Wealth, and that show was dedicated to the problems of the rural areas. Every time a singer would appear on those shows. I myself appeared eight times on that particular show before the war. There was a cultural association, Sloga, which at that time was called Vladimir Nazor and it was active in Prud. I was their active member and, as such, I participated in many international shows, some of them in Italy, Switzerland, and Macedonia, Serbia, Croatia. We went everywhere. We sang everywhere. In simple words, I was a very active in that part, and that is where everybody knew me by my nickname, Solaja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were a member of the Vladimir Nazor cultural association from the village of Prud, did you have to wear a folk -- the Croat folk costume?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly the folk costume that I wore. It was a beautiful folk costume, very rich. And wherever we went, it attracted the attention of the audience, because it was really very, very rich in colours. And whenever there -- at some other cultural events, I would also wear the Serbian folk costume, and I sang. But whenever I went on tours with the cultural society of Prud, I would always wear the Croatian folk costume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a performer of the original folk music, Mr. Zaric, did you participate in celebrations, in religious festivities, in weddings, in sending off boys to the army?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a regular thing. I can even say that there could hardly an event be organised at which I did not participate, at which I did not sing, at which I did not make my contribution. Weddings, christenings. I sang several times when Catholic priests were ordained. There is a very special ceremony when a Catholic priest is ordained, and when he delivers his first mass. This is a huge event. And several times I sang songs at those events. I would also like to say that a number of times people from the party, party members, would call me to task because of my hobby, because they were of the opinion that the political activity and the singing of folk songs cannot go together, but I nevertheless continued doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You participated in all sorts of events of all the ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Sehovici, in a well-known cultural event. I participated together with well-known singers of Muslim folk songs, together with the Begic brothers and a number of people from all ethnic backgrounds who also were involved in that kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. We will move on to another topic. You've already told us that you took an early retirement, that you were forced to retire early, and you told us about the conditions under which you were retired. Can you please tell us now what you did after you were retired, and what were your activities? So what did you do from the 1st of October onwards? I would like to cover the period up to the establishment of the 4th Detachment, the 5th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I was very young when I had to retire. I was still strong. I was going strong. And at the beginning I dedicated my time to stabilise myself, to recharge my batteries, and that's why I helped my family work on the farm in Trnjak. And I also helped my wife, who at the time managed a private grocery store. So I was helping both of the sides, my mother and my wife, and that's how I spent most of my time. And then the municipal secretariat for National Defence mobilised me, and I started working as a reservist, gathering intelligence for the Yugoslav People's Army in the same area where I had previously been the chief of detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you perform these duties? Who were your contacts with and who gave you your orders and your tasks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: My first conversation about that was in the command of the 17th Corps in Tuzla, in the presence of the commander of that corps, General Savo Jankovic, and the chief of the security of that corps, Colonel Musulovic also attended that meeting. Another person who attended was the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel at that time Stevan Nikolic and Captain Petrovic was also there. He was from the Yugoslav People's Garrison in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zaric, what did you discuss at the time with the people who you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I forgot to say that there was also Milos Bogdanovic there at the time. He was the municipal secretary for National Defence. And I have to be honest with you and say that those people had heard that I had been forced to retire overnight, but they also knew that I was very good at what I did and that I was very professional in what I did. And then they told me that I would be mobilised to work on gathering intelligence and necessary for the Yugoslav People's Army in that area. They told me that this intelligence was important to preserve the Yugoslav People's Army as the defence component in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina as an administrative unit of the former Yugoslavia, and to preserve Yugoslavia, which to my mind was the best country in the world and my favourite country in the world ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose that you have accepted those tasks. Did you perform them later on?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did carry out those tasks. I would like to say that nothing was different in the method of work. I didn't apply anything new with regard to what I had done before. When I was retired, I was still a reserve officer for the defence preparation of the SDB of Samac municipality. It's a normal procedure. Once you cease to be an active officer, you become a reserve officer, and that department is the department for preparation -- defence preparation of the SDB. The chief of that was Boro Cvijanovic who was my previous colleague from the SDB detachment in Modrica. I was using my network of associates that I had established as the chief of the service. When I collected my basic intelligence I used to find out how best I could preserve the component of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Yugoslav People's Army, all in view of creating the best possible relationship in order to avoid the evil that had struck Slovenia and Croatia at the beginning of the war there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I would kindly ask you to say something about the reserve department for the defence preparations of the SDB. Is that department a department that had its office in the Bosanski Samac SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This department always had its separate office in the -- on the premises of the public security station. That office was always locked. There was a desk there and some of our technical equipment was there, the equipment that we used as the state security service. And that technique was somewhat different than the technique and technical means used by the public security service. And obviously this department for defence preparations, that was its official establishment title, it belonged to the sector and it was linked up to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but can you please explain to the Honourable Chamber the intelligence that you gathered as the department. Who did you forward this intelligence to? You mentioned Mr. Boro Cvijanovic. Was that the link that you had?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Precisely. When we had our meetings, there were seven of us in that department for defence preparations, and one of those people were Mr. Petar Karlovic, who testified before this Chamber. There was also Mr. Goran Kljajic, who is Mr. Dragan Lukac's brother-in-law, and Dragan Lukac testified before this Chamber. There was also Fikret Sejakovic. What I'm saying is we were of a mixed ethnic composition, our department was. The intelligence that we gathered in the field, we would brief our chief. Our chief would make note of our briefing and then he would inform his superiors in the SDB sector of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps just clarify for the transcript when this was? It's a little bit unclear as to whether it was post-retirement or before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought the witness had explained that this was after retirement when he joined the 4th Detachment and was assigned these duties. Perhaps Mr. Pisarevic can ask the accused to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I started asking you questions along these lines, I said that we were talking about the period of time from the 1st of October, when he was retired, and to the 5th of January, 1992, when the 4th Detachment was established. Mr. Zaric, we were talking about your activities in this department for defence preparations. All this refers to the period between the time you were retired and --?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Between the point of my retirement up to the beginning of April 1992, immediately before the beginning of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you perform your duties towards the Yugoslav People's Army? Who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I reported to the Yugoslav People's Army in drafting reports in one copy, and I would report to my superior in the 17th Tactical Group, Mr. Makso Simeunovic. And before Mr. Makso Simeunovic, there was Mr. Zvonko Jurevic, who was the chief of the OB in the 17th Tactical Group, because Mr. Simeunovic joined the 17th Tactical Group somewhat later. Before he arrived, it was Mr. Zvonko Jurevic, who received the intelligence data from me, those that I deemed significant. And they spoke about the movement of certain forces, about some phenomenon that I recorded in the area of Posavina, and to my mind, those threatened to jeopardise the Yugoslav People's Army or the constitutional order of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, let's conclude by saying -- if I understood you well, you had two jobs at the time. One was for the state security, and the other was for the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Exactly. That was precisely the case. But both institutions were -- belonged to the state, because the Yugoslav People's Army was something that I considered the only legitimate defence force in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the state security was obviously the state security of that state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we're now going to talk about the meetings which preceded the establishment of the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army. Before this Tribunal, we've heard testimonies about that, about the secretariat for National Defence of Samac municipality having organised two meetings with the officers and non-commissioned officers of the JNA in order to inform them about the political and security situation in the area. At those meetings, one -- and these was Colonel Nikolic. My question to you is as follows: Did you also attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start with first meeting first. Can you please tell us when this first meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, both meetings, the first one and the second one, were held in late 1991. The first meeting was held in early November and the second meeting was sometime towards the end of that year. Both meetings were held in the Mitra Trifunovic Vucar [phoen] centre. They were organised by the municipal secretariat for National Defence. All the reserve officers and non-commissioned officers were invited, those were the Samac municipality. Amongst others, Mr. Stevan Nikolic, Lieutenant Colonel, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, with his chief of staff, Brajkovic and some other associated, attended this meeting. At this moment, I can't remember all the names, but I am certain about the two that I've mentioned. The subject, the topic of that meeting was how to organise the defence component in the town of Samac, with a view to preventing the war from the Republic of Croatia spreading in that area, with a view to preventing interethnic conflicts of a large -- at a large scale, if the police was unable to deal with that problem themselves. And also one of the goals was for Bosnia and Herzegovina and this part of the territory to remain an integral part of the former Yugoslavia. These were the three main messages that could be heard at that meeting. I don't want to go into any greater detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. And the secretary of the municipal secretariat for National Defence, Milos Bogdanovic, was he also at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have already said that the meeting was organised by the municipal secretariat, because they were the ones who sent out the invitations. They were the ones who had the record of all the officers and non-commissioned officers. And I remember well that Mr. Milos Bogdanovic attended that meeting, and I have to say that Mr. Bozo Ninkovic also attended the meeting. At that time, he discharged one of the important duties in the secretariat of the National Defence, but I don't know whether he was a deputy or maybe he had some operational duty in that secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we have reached the time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting the testimony, very briefly. Before Mr. Zaric started testifying, I wanted to address you with regard to the submission of the Prosecution with regard to Mr. Jovan Erletic, but I had to take advantage of the break to confer with my colleague. Since we have been instructed to express our position by today, I would just like to briefly say that Mr. Miroslav Tadic's Defence counsel doesn't have the intention of cross-examining Mr. Jovan Erletic. This is all I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber of. I didn't want to submit anything in writing about this matter. I wanted to follow the Trial Chamber's instructions about oral addresses. And with regard to the Prosecution's position, we will not be cross-examining Mr. Jovan Erletic, given the contents of his statement. This is what I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On the same matter, we would like to have this witness for cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which one? What's the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Erletic, the last one. Because you already ruled with regard to the presence of Witness Marko Tubakovic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we are speaking about Mr. Erletic. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We'll proceed, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, just a brief instruction. I have been asked by the interpreters to ask you if you could slow down slightly. It's in your interest to speak a little more slowly, because that will enable them to do their work properly. So could you please try to speak a little more slowly.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We were speaking about the first meeting in the centre, organised by the secretariat for National Defence in the municipality of Samac, and I would now like to ask you if you can remember anything about this: Who took the floor at that meeting? That's my first question. Because at that meeting of the reserve officers and non-commissioned officers, Milos Bogdanovic, as the secretary of the secretariat for National Defence, he spoke at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Stevan Nikolic, take the floor at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can remember, can you tell us what Colonel Stevan Nikolic, as commander of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA, can you tell us what he told the reserve officers and non-commissioned officers who were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, I would first of all like to inform the Trial Chamber to compare the speakers. If we're talking about Milos Bogdanovic, who was the secretariat of the municipal secretariat, he only made introductory remarks and explained the reasons for which we were gathered. Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, took the floor. Igor Kobas [as interpreted], the commander of the municipal staff of the Samac municipality, took the floor at that time. I spoke briefly at that meeting. Mr. Esad Delic also spoke, Captain first class, and there were several other people who spoke, who took the floor. It wasn't just a matter of simply issuing instructions and information. There was, so to speak, a more open discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One correction for the transcript. On page 34, line 2, the name was Ivo Kobas, and he was actually the commander of the municipal staff of the TO of Samac municipality. Just to have this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: To summarise what some of them said, I can point out that the main message of Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic was that it was essential to organise a defence within the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. At the time he did not conceal the fact that the Territorial Defence was not performing the function that it was supposed to perform, and Ivo Kobas in particular addressed this matter and he pointed to the impossibility of organising the Territorial Defence in the way that it was supposed to be organised, according to the constitution in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because many officers, non-commissioned officers and soldiers, failed to respond to the summons as issued by the municipal staff for legitimate defence units to be formed, and according to the BH constitution and the law on national defence, such units were supposed to be formed. Mr. Stevan Nikolic's main message was that what the television programme showed from the territory of Slovenia and Croatia was quite sufficient to show the evil spread by war, and everything should be done to make sure that the way the war was being presented from Croatia, it shouldn't be presented in Bosnia and Herzegovina in that way. He asked for unity, freedom among the officers and non-commissioned officers, and he requested that they help maintain order, maintain harmony among the people, and he requested that there should not be interethnic conflicts on a large scale in this area of ours. He drew attention to certain very complex security elements which were present in the Posavina area, from Bosanski Brod right up to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, at the time, did Mr. Nikolic ask all officers and non-commissioned officers, regardless of their ethnic membership, did he request that they join the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. In a very manifest and clear way, and I quite clearly remember his words, and this is a well-known fact. It was easy to organise a certain kind of defence in villages inhabited by Serbs, where the Serbs were in the majority or where the Croats were in the majority. It was a problem how to organise defence in a town in which people of all ethnic groups lived. That was the main problem, which is why he made an appeal and he requested that all officers and non-commissioned officers who were prepared to defend such a conception, who were prepared to defend the city, he asked them to report to the secretariat of -- for National Defence. He asked them to mobilise. And then it was the responsibility of the municipal secretariat for National Defence to compile certain records. And on the basis of those records, to proceed to organise certain units, and also to organise the 4th Detachment, of which more will be said in the future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but there is -- on page 35, line 7, there is an expression which perhaps is due to the translation. It reads: "That they help maintain order, maintain harmony among the people, and he" - that means Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic - "requested that there should not be interethnic conflicts on a large scale in this area of ours." That expression "on a large scale" must -- it's very ambiguous what is meant. Is it that he accepted, so to say, on a small -- on a minor scale but not on a large scale? Could you clarify that with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you have heard the question. I think it has to do with the translation, after all. What did Mr. Nikolic request? How did he want the reserve military officers to become engaged? What sort of contribution did he want them to make?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: When I used the word "large scale," when I was testifying before the break, I clarified this matter to a certain extent, I was referring to, and I think that Mr. Nikolic was referring to the same thing, I was thinking about certain ethnic conflicts not being able to be controlled by the police and the army. I was thinking of serious incidents that couldn't be controlled by the police. And then in such a case, the army's role would be obvious. In such a case, the army would have to assume a position. But the army didn't tolerate any serious incidents. Mr. Nikolic was only pointing to certain details, and I'll talk about these details later on, because they're part of the security problem in that area. He was just drawing attention to the fact that those details, events in various parts of Posavina, could make the situation more complex and could make it difficult to control the political and security situation. That's what I was thinking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you said that you too participated in that first meeting, you also took the floor. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember, before this Trial Chamber here today, the matters you spoke about at that meeting? Could you be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I took advantage of the opportunity, because the people who were at that meeting, the officers and the non-commissioned officers who were there, knew me quite well, and they knew that I had worked in the security service for years. Perhaps many at the time were not aware of the fact that I had been retired. I pointed to the complex security situation in the Posavina area, and in particular in the area of Samac, Modrica, Orasje areas, and I referred to certain events. I knew that these things were happening for sure, and I said that it was necessary to organise a unified defence, not only in the town of Samac. I spoke about it necessary to having a unified defence in the area of the entire municipality of Samac, and beyond that area too. And this was borne out by subsequent events. It would have been of no significance if Samac had joint defence and other rural areas had other military formations, other armies. In such a case, this would not have improved the situation. This would only have made the security situation deteriorate. So that is the matter that I addressed, because we knew each other, and our main task was to remain unified in the town of Samac, because Samac was also the administrative centre of the municipality, where all the key institutions were located: The industry, et cetera, in the municipality area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, did you appeal to all officers and non-commissioned officers to join the JNA, regardless of the ethnic groups they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was the principle that I followed, and this is a principle that I will adhere to at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now turn to the other meeting held in December. You said that at that meeting -- that that meeting was also held in the memorial centre. Who was present at the meeting, and what did you notice at that meeting with regard to the presence of officers and non-commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: All I can say is that the first and second meetings were held -- that the first and second meeting were held in the hall, the so-called red hall of the memorial centre. It's called the red hall because the seats in the hall had red upholstery. I can remember very well that there were between 60 and 70 officers and non-commissioned officers from the town of Samac. And on the second time the meeting was held in December, a third of that number was present. About 70 per cent of that third were Serbian nationality. The others were Muslims and Croats. I apologise -- who had responded to that appeal. And it is thus possible to conclude that the appeal made at the first meeting didn't bear any fruit. Many officers and non-commissioned officers, in my opinion, followed national leaders rather than us from the defence unit that I have spoken about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the matters discussed at the second meeting at the memorial centre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The subject-matter was very similar at the second meeting, and it was indicated that there was a mood in town, there was the will to form a defence, and an agreement was reached to mobilise, to carry out the voluntary mobilisation of all men liable for military service who wanted to join such a defence unit. So the tasks -- the objectives would be the same as the ones that I have spoken about here. There was nothing else apart from the fact that the people from the secretariat for National Defence made a record of those who were present at the second meeting, and they counted on those officers and non-commissioned officers for organising a unit which would be established as of January, as a certain unit in the area of the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that a unit would be formed. Tell us: What was the nature of the unit that was formed? What was its name and when was it established?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: This united was called the 4th Detachment of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. In territorial terms, it was linked to the Samac settlement alone, and it was part of the 17th Tactical Group, under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, and its headquarters was in Pelagici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the 4th Detachment established?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: By order of the command of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, it was established on the 5th of January, 1992. The decision was adopted on forming the 4th Detachment. Its principal leadership was appointed and its leadership was assigned with the task of gradually organising subordinate and other necessary military units which would form the detachment, which would compose the detachment as a unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you become a member of the 4th Detachment? How did this take place and when did it take place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: When this order was issued, the one that I mentioned a minute ago, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic appointed a detachment commander, and from the 5th of January, 1992, I officially became a member of that detachment and I had the duties of the -- as assistant commander for security and information affairs and for information and morale. This additional function was given this name later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Who was appointed as commander of the 4th Detachment by Stevan Nikolic's order?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Captain first class Mr. Radovan Antic was appointed as commander of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was appointed as deputy commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Deputy commander of the 4th Detachment, as deputy commander of the 4th Detachment, Mr. Jovo Savic, who was also a Captain first class, was appointed to this post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Miroslav Tadic also appointed a certain position by virtue -- by this order?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the deputy commander of the 4th Detachment for logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just told us that you were appointed as a deputy commander for security and intelligence affairs, according to the order issued by lieutenant colonel. Could you now tell us what your duties and tasks included, as deputy commander for security and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: When the decision was adopted on establishing the 4th Detachment, I was given these security duties in addition to my other duties, and this in fact meant that I should monitor all intelligence, that I should gather all intelligence that might relate to threats, to the existence of that unit. I had monitored the security situation in that area, in the area of the town, where our zone of responsibility had been established. I was to gather all kinds -- all sorts of information in intelligence that might be of interest. And intelligence on units that were against the establishment of that detachment. So it had to do with protecting intelligence and also counter-intelligence. So very briefly, those would be my duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what sort of authority did you have? Did you have any kind of authority as part of your duties that you had to perform?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The deputy commander of the detachment is on the lower step of the hierarchy in security terms in the JNA, and in the Territorial Defence too. There are no -- lower [as interpreted] units in the detachment don't have that security component. So my task was to gather such intelligence and to relay such intelligence to my superior, Makso Simeunovic, who was the chief of the intelligence and security organ of the 17th Tactical Group. So I was authorised to gather intelligence, information, and to relay this intelligence. Some of the intelligence was intelligence that I relayed to Mr. Simeunovic, and other parts of the information I would relay to the commander of the 4th Detachment, Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The exact word that Mr. Zaric used here on page 41, line 23, is the lowest step of the hierarchy, and here it says "lower." The lowest. That was the word he used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you have any command role in the detachment, i.e., did you have the right to issue any orders to anybody, to any of the members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have any command role along these lines. I did not have any authorities along these lines. This is not envisaged by any regulations, nor did I have such a role in reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who in the command of the 4th Detachment had the authority to issue executive orders to the members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The authority to issue such orders belonged to the commander of the 4th Detachment, Mr. Radovan Antic. In case of his absence, some of the executive orders could be issued by his deputy, Captain Jovo Savic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Zaric, have any authority, either given to you by the commander or the deputy commander of the detachment, to issue any kind of executive orders?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have any such authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Irrespective of that, did you yourself, Mr. Zaric, ever issue any executive order to any of the members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I will ask you to answer a few questions relative to the functioning of the security organs of the 4th Detachment. One of them would be who was your superior? Who were you subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I was subordinated to the commander of the detachment. That was down the line of commandment and the line of subordination. My immediate superior was the chief of the security in the 17th Tactical Group, Mr. Makso Simeunovic, which means that one needs to bear in mind these two communication components. One goes along the line or the chain of command, to which I'm linked directly -- according to which I'm directly linked to the commander of the detachment, and with that, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, and according to the lines of subordination and the conveying of the intelligence information, my first immediate superior was my -- was Mr. Makso Simeunovic, as the chief of the intelligence and security at the level of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you report to, Mr. Zaric, about your work?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I sent a written report and I gave oral reports to my superior, Mr. Makso Simeunovic. Some of the intelligence which I believe they were of vital interest for the security of the detachment, I would give directly to the commander of the detachment, Mr. Nikolic, or - sorry - Mr. Antic, the commander of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you submitted your report or when you conveyed certain information to your superior - according to the principles of subordination, that was Mr. Makso Simeunovic - was Mr. Makso Simeunovic under the obligation to inform you about what happened with your report and the intelligence that you gathered?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. Once I issued my report to Mr. Makso Simeunovic, he was under no obligation to give me any feedback on what the lot of my information or my report was. But it did happen that some significant intelligence was discussed or I would receive some new task that stemmed from that piece of intelligence. However, he was under no obligation to give me any feedback on what I gave him as intelligence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that in addition to the security and intelligence tasks in the detachment, you also performed some tasks that were relative to morale and information. Tell me: Who issued the orders to you about the morale and the information in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
