utterances.text: When the command of the detachment was established, it was immediately said that in addition to the intelligence and security, I would also be in charge of the duties relative to the information and morale in the unit. In simple words, this meant I would be the port parole [phoen] [Realtime transcript read in error "corporal"] of that unit. And when I received my orders in that segment, that was from the commander Antic or his deputy Mr. Savic. And when I appeared on two occasions in the public, that was done at the express order of Commander Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now describe for the Trial Chamber what were the contents of your tasks relative to the issues of morale in the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: When the decision was adopted on establishing the 4th Detachment, an attempt was immediately made to do a trial and see how many people would respond to this mobilisation, the tasks and goals were of which -- of which were as I explained a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Clarification on page 44, line 20. In simple words, this means that I would be the corporal. Actually, Mr. Zaric said "port parole" [phoen]. This was the word that he used, the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning already in January, over 200 men responded to the mobilisation call. They were of all ethnic backgrounds and they wanted to join this detachment. Very soon after that, we decided to stage a public meeting with the first group of people who volunteered and responded to the mobilisation call. And one of my tasks at that meeting, which was amongst others attended by Mr. Nikolic and by Mr. Antic, so one of my tasks was to exert moral influence, to exert influence and try and mobilise as many people as possible to join this defence component whose name was the 4th Detachment. My message was that it was the only guarantee for the safety of our town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your duties relative to information in the detachment, what were they all about? Let's first consider the issue of providing information to the members of the 4th Detachment. How did -- how was that organised? Were there any regular meetings with those people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were meetings on a large scale, with all the members, and smaller-scale meetings in units. There was three or four meetings, one of them in the memorial centre, another one in the Tekstilac restaurant. Tekstilac is the Samac textile industry, which also housed the command of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the topics that you discussed at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The main topic was to point to the members of the 4th Detachment how serious the political and the security situation was at that time, not only in the town and municipality of Samac but also in the general area. The message was also to point out the need to establish a defence component in order to resist everything that looked like war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us now: Who were the speakers at the meetings of the members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: At the meeting which was held in the memorial centre, one of the speakers was Mr. Stevan Nikolic, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, whose speech conveyed the messages that I've already mentioned. Another speaker was Mr. Radovan Antic, who was the commander of the detachment, and also several members of the unit, people who raised certain issues, who wanted to know how the detachment would be organised and how the defence component of the 4th Detachment would develop. One of the speakers was also myself, and I've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously you were one of the speakers, and what did you emphasise? What messages did you convey to the members of the 4th Detachment? Was your goal to inform the people about the situation in the general area in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Already at that time, we had at our disposal information about several incidents that had happened and that had shown us that the situation, both in town and in the general area of Samac municipality, was getting more complex by the day. We mentioned all those incidents, and we wanted to show people how complex the situation was and what the final outcome of that situation might be. On the other hand, in the political and public life of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a very complex drama was evolving. There was an ethnic drift, and the parliamentary system in Bosnia and Herzegovina was blocked. Those incidents in our area deserved to be mentioned to the members of the unit. The underlying idea was to tell them that there was no other possibility for us to defend ourselves from the evil but to be united in our defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. Let's move on to the question of providing information to the general public in Bosanski Samac, about the existence and the goals of the detachment. Did any of you appear in the media or in meetings? Did any of you inform the general public about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were public appearances which took place in two ways. Firstly, there was an official information on behalf of the general secretariat for National Defence about a defence component, under the name of the 4th Detachment of the JNA, having been formed in Samac. It was said that this unit was organised and that it comprised of people from all ethnic groups. And the second way of conveying information was a round table, a public round table, in Radio Samac. I was one of the participants of that round table. I participated on behalf of the 4th Detachment. Another participant was Vinko Dragicevic, on behalf of the public security station. Commanders Antic participated on behalf of the 4th Detachment. And I believe there was also Mr. Milos Bogdanovic, on behalf of the secretariat for National Defence. And we, as such, answered a number of people who phoned in and wanted to raise questions with that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Zaric. You said that there was a round table. Does that mean that you participated in radio shows and you talked about the existence of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said who were other participants in that show. What did you say on that show? What did you personally say? Did you again appeal and mention the need to be united?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did convey exactly that message. Unity was something that I always fostered, and whenever I appeared in public, I could not not mention unity, because that's the only way I could talk. That was my life motive, unity of all peoples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you -- you always said that it was a live show. Does that mean that people could phone in, that listeners could directly ask questions to all the participants of the show?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could be done. There were some very delicate issues raised, because there had been a number of incidents that preceded that show. Some of those happened in Samac, Bosanski Brod, Orasje. And would we -- we could say in very honest terms, we would answer the questions, all of us, Mr. Antic, Mr. Dragicevic, and myself. We tried to answer all of these questions in a very honest manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zaric, did you appear at meetings of citizens on various occasions on behalf of the 4th Detachment of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: How many such meetings did you attend, and how many times you appeared in such meetings.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The majority of these meetings took place in the area of the town of Samac. Those were attended by members of the 4th Detachment. But I must also say that all of our public meetings could be attended by any citizen who was of military age. And listen to what we were talking about. We never kept anything concealed from the general public. We didn't -- we never refrained from talking about our goals. Many of the people who attended those meetings, we knew that they had already been members of some paramilitary units organised by their respective parties. But our message was always clear, and we always pointed out the things that I have just spoken about. I want to say something else. Not only as a member of the 4th Detachment, but also as -- in other capacities, I participated in some peace rallies in Prud, Vojskova, and Kornica, and I had the opportunity to talk about that at those rallies. And my only goal was to defend the unity of the Yugoslav People's Army and the unity of those peoples who resided in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Thank you. I'm going to ask you a question. We will go back to this subject again at a later stage, but now I'd like to ask you this: Were there any meetings with the representatives of the Bosanski Samac local commune, and did you attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were very many such meetings and very many times I participated in those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll come back to that later. And now let's move on to the political and security situation in Samac municipality during the period between the 1st of October, 1991, and the 17th of April, 1992. We're talking about the period of time between the 1st of October, 1991, and the 17th of April, 1992. Can you give us a short overview of that situation in Samac municipality, and then we will go into details of various events that occurred during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I can say that during that period between the 1st of October and the outbreak of conflicts, because of various incidents that were taking place from Bosanski Brod to Brcko, that part of Posavina was a little Beirut, and especially Samac. When I say Beirut, I mean that there were almost daily sabotage and terrorist actions of all sorts, which jeopardised the political and security situation and contributed towards the political polarisation in the territory of Posavina and in the general area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. As far as you can remember, which sabotage actions by their force and by their consequences made the situation more complex? What sabotage actions took place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I don't know how fair it is going to be, but I would like to inform the Honourable Chamber what happened before the 1st of October. There were two situations which I believe were relevant. Before I was retired, there was one incident in July, and the other one was in August, immediately before I was retired. So I'm talking about the time when I was still the active chief of the service. The first incident took place in the village of Obudovac, the largest Serbian village in the territory of Samac municipality. We learnt about an illegal operation of smuggling of hunting rifles. The intelligence was gathered together with the state security and the public security services, and we arrived at the conclusion that these hunting rifles were bought and resold for material gain. They were not bought to serve as a deterrent against anybody or as -- in order to threaten somebody. Those rifles were bought at hundred German marks and sold at two or three hundred German marks. This was published in the security bulletin of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it went down with a bang, and a huge security impact was given to that case. And I have just told you the way I saw that incident. It was nothing but a small-scale smuggling. The second security incident took place at the end of August, when an illegal contingent of weapons arrived in Modrica. This was organised by the HDZ, and the weapons were produced in the Djuro Djakovic company in Slavonski Brod. These weapons were Zagi automatic weapon, and the Sokac automatic weapon. Zagi and Sokac were their popular names. Through my network of associates, I managed to break this smuggling canal on the other side in Kladari, Garevac villages, in the territory of Modrica municipality, these were things were supposed to be given to the HOS paramilitary formation. Those were the Croatian defence forces which were based in the Republic of Croatia and their commander was Dobrislav Paraga. I must say that at that point in time, when we were able to intercept this operation, something happened in our service and this was interrupted. I was very angry. I reacted to that at our meeting in Doboj. And I'm not saying that this was the only reason, but certainly one of the reasons for which I was forced to retire prematurely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, then, Mr. Zaric. Let's go back to my original question, and that was about the sabotage actions that took place in Samac municipality during the period between the 1st of October and the 17th of -- that is, the 1st of October, 1991, and the 17th of April, 1992. What sabotage operations or actions took place during that time, and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: There were a number of those sabotage actions, one worse than the other. The first such sabotage actions took place at the very beginning of December 1991. I'm not going to draw any inferences. That should be the task of somebody else. But at the beginning of December, a special unit of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina arrived in the territory of Samac. Their commanders were Besirevic, Safet and Hodzic Ragib and they arrived on the 2nd of December, and they had about a hundred specials with them, all members of the Ministry of the Interior. Their task was primarily to provide security for the bridge on the Sava River. At that time, that was the only possibility to cross the Sava River and that was the only connection between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And their task was also to look after the security component in the territory of the municipalities of Samac and Odzak.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: (redacted) . Maybe if the Trial Chamber will allow me, I can mention their names in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we briefly go into closed session so that the names of these people around mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we can go in private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, were there any other privately owned buildings that were blown up in the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: In December, December was a month during which many incidents occurred, both private and public incidents. As far as I can remember, on the 9th of December, the nuclear shelter in the Hranaprodukt food factory was destroyed and there were over 540 missiles, anti-hail missiles there. Kapetanovic's summer house was destroyed, which was located in the direction of Tursinovac. It was outside the Samac area. On the 14th of February, the business premises of Muharem Bajraktarevic was destroyed. He's a Muslim from Samac. It was a building that hadn't been completed. Explosives were planted there and damage was inflicted on that building. And on the same day, a little later, that notorious incident in the Valentino Cafe occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Zaric. I just want to just clarify one thing. It might be a matter of translation. On page 54, lines 18 to 21, Mr. Zaric's answer speaks about the nuclear shelter in the Hranaprodukt food factory was destroyed and there were over 540 missiles there. Is that correct? It just reads a little oddly to me. Maybe you could clarify with Mr. Zaric, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you have heard Judge Williams' question. Missiles, rockets were mentioned. It's obvious that -- what sort of rockets are at stake, the ones that were located in the nuclear shelter in the food company?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: These are anti-hail missiles, rockets. That is their name. These are rockets that are used if there's a ferocious storm. These rockets are launched from launch pads in order to disperse the clouds and to prevent the storm from inflicting damage on the city. In wartime conditions, when these rockets are placed on launch pads, they only perform a psychological role. Their purpose is to frighten people. Because when you put them one next to the other, you have the impression that what is involved is a multiple rocket launcher. So this was one of the biggest and most modern nuclear shelters in the municipality of Samac. It was a new factory, and in that nuclear shelter, that's what it was called, there were over 540 anti-hail missiles, anti-hail rockets. And there is one other thing that I should inform Judge Williams of. When the explosion occurred, it was terrible to observe, because Samac was practically covered by cloud. Those rockets don't -- aren't fired all at once, but in succession. They can't all be fired at once. They are fired in succession. So you can imagine when 540-odd rockets exploded, it was something that was quite frightening for the people who observed the event, and this factory was located on the outskirts of the town, at a certain distances from the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we just be a little more precise about those rockets. In fact, these rockets used for weather purposes, meteorological rockets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Were buildings damaged, bridges, power lines, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: In December, as far as I know, several power lines were destroyed. One of the biggest power lines was near the bridge, in the immediate vicinity of the bridge over the Sava, and it was guarded by the special police units from Sarajevo. And on that same evening, Nedic Marko's disco, called Miler was destroyed. It's on the main road from Samac to the village of Obudovac. The second power line that was destroyed was in the direction of Lugovi. It is sort of an agricultural location and in a certain sense all the Serbian villages were cut off. I don't want to go into the details, but Mr. Alija Fitozovic has testified about this in very clear terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Were there any other events in the seriousness of which contributed to a feeling of insecurity and which contributed to divisions among the people, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: In February, I think - I don't know whether it was on the 4th or the 5th of February, but it was one of those two days, that is certain - significant damage was inflicted on the bridge over the River Sava, and that was the only functioning bridge at the time that connected the Republic of Croatia with Bosnia-Herzegovina. And what is very indicative, in my opinion, with regard to the destruction of this bridge is the fact that it was blown up at 8.45 in the morning. And before that time, the chief of the police, of the public security service, stopped traffic on both sides of the bridge. That is when the explosion occurred. Fortunately, no significant casualties, and the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina condemned the behaviour of Chief Dragicevic and those who were guarding that bridge. They characterised this act in very particular terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small clarification to give sense to what we have here as the answer of Mr. Zaric: "And before that time, at 8.00." There is one part of the sentence missing here. So 45 minutes before it happened, the police stopped traffic to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zaric, maybe you can go over that slowly so that it's correctly recorded. THE ACCUSED ZARIC: [Interpretation] When the explosion occurred on the 5th of February, according to the information I had, the explosion took place at 8.45 in the morning, and at 8.00 in the morning the chief of security ordered that there should no longer be any traffic over the bridge. There is a written report, a communique, about this, because a commission from the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina came to carry out an on-site investigation to determine how this occurred. And I was in a position to see that document. And the media provided their own interpretation of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other events which contributed to rendering the situation in the municipality of Bosanski Samac more complex? Were any buildings damaged at the Orthodox cemetery, were there patrols of any kind in the town of Samac? What happened to the Valentino Cafe? Tell us a little more about these events.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of January, 1992, on one of the most significant religious events for the Orthodox people, St. Sava, the Orthodox chapel was blown up, in the Orthodox cemetery. This chapel was used when someone was brought there to be buried. The people were very much embittered by this event, all the more so in that this occurred on that religious day, and the public didn't fail to comment on this. I mentioned Mr. Safet Besirevic and Ragib Hodzic. According to reliable information that I had when I was involved in these duties, I knew that they were instructors in the Patriotic League of Bosnia and Herzegovina, headed by Sefer Halilovic. They spent more time on the premises of the Party of Democratic Action, more time there than on the premises of the Ministry of the Interior, and they were very often there with Mr. Alija Fitozovic. And from February onwards, they -- from February onwards, Muslim patrols started patrolling the town. Their purpose was allegedly to protect buildings owned by Muslims. This was an issue that was often discussed at the Crisis Staff of the local commune, and I too participated in these discussions on behalf of the 4th Detachment, representatives for all the political parties in the town and at the municipality level also participated, representatives of the police, the ministry of the defence, and I know that Mr. Sulejman Tihic was in favour of the legitimacy of these SDA patrols. And my opinion at these meetings was that this should be done by having recourse to the reserve police force. And those were the differences that we had. I didn't think that it should be done. On a private basis, I thought that there should be mixed patrols of the reserve police force. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we will address these issues later on, but at the moment we are discussing the events that made the political and security situation in the municipality of Samac more complex, from the 1st of October -- from the 2nd of October until the 16th or 17th of April, 1992. Were there any other events that gave some significance and contributed to endangering the security and political situation and the relations between ethnic groups, not only in the town of Samac but also in the municipality itself?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I went off on a tangent when I wanted to speak of these patrols, but it is because the military police, on one occasion, in March, disarmed one such patrol, one such SDA patrol, not far from the Mebos factory. That was a reason allegedly to erect barricades and to prohibit anyone else entering the town. The Party of Democratic Action was responsible for organising the erection of these barricades and this action was led by Mr. Alija Fitozovic, and he has confirmed this fact in his testimony before this Trial Chamber. But the barricades themselves contributed to a certain security situation which was negative in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Where were these barricades erected?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: At the two main entrances to the town of Samac, although there was, so to speak, an additional third barricade. But as far as the first two are concerned, one was placed when you enter Bosanski Samac from the direction of Nedrici [phoen]. It was by the Mebos factory, at the entrance to the Mebos factory, by the brick factory. And the second barricade was at the crossroads near Uzarija, which you would approach from Orasje and Obudovac, via the main road. So from that direction, no Serbs or members of other peoples were allowed to enter the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I can just have one small clarification. On page 60, line 7, there was an additional third entrance. Mr. Zaric was referring to the entrances to the town of Samac, not to the third barricade. So the barricades were placed on two entrances, and a third one was free.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you tell us about the third entrance to Samac, where there were no barricades.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: That was an entrance that went in the direction of the village of Prud, over the bridge over the River Bosna and towards my place of birth, the village of Trnjak. At the time there were no barricades on the bridge. But the reserve police of the HDZ was on that side and guarded the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: You said the reserve police, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Who were the people who manned those barricades?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the people manning the barricades were mainly Muslims, and there was a lower number of Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people manning those barricades, did they have automatic weapons, military weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were armed. In addition to the obstructions they had on the road, they used buses, passenger vehicles, and it wasn't possible to pass by them. Quite a few of them were under the influence of alcohol. And fortunately, there were no serious incidents after the intervention of certain political bodies in the town. And Mr. Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group was spoken to about that matter by Mr. Izo Izetbegovic. After these conversations, there were no significant incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, did you ever hear anything about barricades being established at the entrance to the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No. That was the first time. What makes this situation more complex with regard to the barricades is the fact and the reliable information that we had, according to which at the time Mr. Alija Fitozovic had linked those barricades to the mobilisation of paramilitary formations which were located in Croatian local communes alone, and that fact, in my opinion, represented a far greater danger than the fact that teams of alcoholised and irresponsible people claimed the right to decide who could enter the town and who could not enter the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did the 4th Detachment take any action to remove these barricades, and did you inform Commander Stevan Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, of the fact that these barricades had been erected?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, the role of the 4th Detachment was for me to inform Commander Antic, Commander Nikolic, and I had to inform Makso Simeunovic that the town had been -- was under a blockade, and we were immediately informed that the 4th Detachment should not get involved in that, by no means. We were told that this was a matter for the police. It was for them to deal with that, for them and the political organs, and we shouldn't think of doing anything. Commander Antic respected this order, so that the 4th Detachment didn't play any role in removing these barricades, apart from this information, this report I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember the names of some of the men who were involved in these barricades?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Suljic Jadranko was involved in this, Ibrahim Salkic, also known as Ibela, Mesmic Osman [phoen], known as Buca, Dragan Markovic, also known as Mirin; Gibic, also known as Dasa. I'm sure about these men. Naturally, Alija Fitozovic was in command. He went from one checkpoint to the other and he commanded these units. There's no doubt as to the fact that he participated in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. On many occasions we have heard testimony that on the 14th [Realtime transcript read in error "4th"] of February, 1992 - and that's the event in which two Muslim youths were killed in the Valentino Cafe - we have heard testimony about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's a mistake in the transcript. It's not the 4th of February. It's the 14th of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about this event, and what sort of consequences arose in the town of Samac itself? Did this make the relations between ethnic groups more complex? Can you tell us something about this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I was in Obudovac when this happened. I was staying with friends. I was with friends. And when I found out such a serious incident had occurred, I returned to Bosanski Samac immediately. I was informed about this by my wife. She said that people had been dead. Nasim Sireli [as interpreted] was not far from that cafe. Nasim Mirel [as interpreted]. The incident occurred when a bomb exploded in the Valentino Cafe on the day of St. Valentine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I could give some sense to this. There is no Nasim or someone. Mr. Zaric, in B/C/S, "nas sin," this meaning "our son," Mirel. So this is on page 63, line 10. So it's not Nasim Mirel, but it's our son, Mirel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: A bomb exploded on St. Valentine's Day. On that occasion, two young men were killed. One of them was called Hadzialijagic and the other one was called Bobic. A girl was seriously injured. Her name was Pavlovic. And she was going out with that young man, Bobic. Several other young people were wounded. There was panic. And on the same evening there was a spontaneous protest, gathering, organised by -- well, I wouldn't say extremists, but people from the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this gathering, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, it started in front of the hotel, not far from that cafe, immediately, and then the column headed towards the SJB, the public security station in Samac. And I was an eyewitness of that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see in front of the public security station in Samac? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I've been reminded it's time for the break. Maybe we could continue this after the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, the last thing that we mentioned before this break was the rally of citizens in front of the public security station in Bosanski Samac. You were there, as you have already told us. When did you arrive? What did you see? What was going on in front of the public security station in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: According to my estimate, there were about 300 or 400 people there. It was a respectable number, I would say. They were very loud, expressing their dissatisfaction with the Yugoslav People's Army, with Serbs in general, with Chetniks and so on and so forth. So it was very unpleasant to listen to some of those individuals and the way they blamed some people for the incident that had happened in that cafe. I went through this group of people. I entered the building. It was not a problem for me. My colleagues knew that I had free access, because I had my office there and I had free access to that office. In my conversation with Mr. Lukac there, and in my conversation with Mr. Milos Savic and Zoran Jovanovic, who was a technician in the service, very soon I learnt that this had been just an accident, a stupid accident, nothing else, that this guy, Bobic, had a grenade in his possession and that he activated it by accident. He got scared. He gave the grenade to the guy called Hadzialijagic and the tragedy occurred, just like that. Upstairs in Chief Dragicevic's office, there was Safet Hadzialijagic also, known as Coner. He is the uncle of one of the dead persons of the guy called Hadzialijagic. Based on the initial information, Mr. Dragicevic told him what this has been all about, and a meeting was staged between Mr. Hadzialijagic and me, before he appeared in front of that large group of people. I expressed my condolences to him, but since I knew that Mr. Safet Hadzialijagic, also known as Coner, had a very strong authority in town, I told him that he had to muster the force to appear before the people at that moment when he knew what this was all about, that he had to exert his authority to calm the people and to tell them to go home and leave it to the competent services to see the matter through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I must say that Safet and I left the building alone and started talking to the people. At the beginning, there were expressions of displeasure, most of them at my address. But that is not important at this moment. Safet raised his hand and this group of people quietened down a bit, and he said something along these lines: There was a huge tragedy, but I kindly ask you to go home. This was nothing but an accident, and we have to place our trust with the competent organs, who will investigate the matter and see the things through. This had a calming effect on the mass. I have to say that I believe that Mr. Hadzialijagic's words were decisive and contributed largely to a peaceful end of the whole situation. But let me just say one more thing. Before I entered the public security station building, the spokesmen, among whom I recognised Jasarevic, also known as Roma, and Blaz Paradzik from Roma [as interpreted], did not choose their words when they were swearing the Serbs, the Chetniks, the army, the SDS. Those were ugly words and very difficult to listen to. But after Mr. Hadzialijagic addressed the people, the people went -- decided to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Blaz Paradzik is from Prud, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Blaz Paradzik is from Prud, and he's one of the witnesses who testified as a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was there with you in front of the public security station when you first got there? Who accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of people, but next to me was Mr. Mlado Sarkanovic. Mr. Mihajlo Topolovac was also with me, Mr. Milos Simendic. My brother-in-law Fadil Topcagic. So these were the people with whom I left that rally eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, where did you go after that when people dispelled and when the situation quietened down a bit? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: First we went to Bobic's house. I don't know whether he was a protected witness before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kemal Bobic. No, he's not.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: First we went to Kemal Bobic's house. He is the father of this guy Bobic who had been killed. Me and especially Mr. Sarkanovic were on very good terms with him. It was our desire to express our condolences to him, to calm him down as much as possible. It was dark. There were a lot of people in his front yard. He received us in a very correct manner. He accepted our condolences, as well as his wife Ediba. She also treated us in a very fair manner. And then a young man turned up, in very coarse words he started insulting us along the same lines of the words that were heard in front of the public security station. He cursed our Serbian mothers, our Chetnik mothers. He blamed Chetniks for everything that happened. He blamed the JNA. And Mr. Bobic told us: Don't pay any attention to him. He is a nervous, agitated type and he is the brother of his wife, a native of Orasje. I replied: I understand. I appreciate that. But if anybody had the strength, they should say that this man that he shouldn't behave in that way. That was my reaction to that outburst.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Your visit to Mr. Kemal Bobic ended?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this visit ended and then I and the same group of people went to Hadzialijagic's house, which is on the way towards the River Sava, towards the River Bosna, and we also expressed our condolences to this guy Hadzialijagic's father and mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there incidents there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: There were no incidents there. Before us, Safet Hadzialijagic, Coner, arrived at that house and it was my assumption that he had already told the family how the accident occurred, and they were prepared and they accepted our condolences in a very fair manner. I did not notice in them any reservations towards our words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, was there any rally of citizens in the town of Bosanski Samac that was provoked by that accident?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where that rally was gathered?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: That rally was staged on the following day, in the afternoon, in the cinema in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, did you also attend that meeting or that rally?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. I participated in the discussion and in the talks that were conducted at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other speakers at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Hadzialijagic, also known as Coner, spoke,; then Mr. Stevo Randzic from the secretariat for National Defence; Mr. Sulejman Tihic; and two more young men also spoke at that meeting. One of them was a Muslim. I'm sure. I don't know his last name. But he talked in rather inflamed words and wanted to turn that rally into something else, but he did not gain much support. But in any case, I know that a few of us participated in -- actively in that meeting. And according to my estimate, the cinema was full. There must have been about a thousand people in that room. The room was completely packed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In very brief outlines, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you said at that meeting, at that rally of citizens of Bosanski Samac which took place in the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I remember well what I said. As far as I know, part of my speech is also part of an exhibit, so I won't go into great length, because I'm sure the Trial Chamber will have the opportunity to read it. But let me paraphrase in as brief as possible outlines. I referred to the programme of the Socialist Democratic Party. I did not use this opportunity as a political stage. I just wanted to point out the fact that its basic messages was for us to live together in harmony, to respect each other, to live in fraternity and unity, and not to allow anybody to put our peace that we enjoyed at stake. I said that the older amongst us have to feel responsible about the grenade being found on such a young person, that we had lost two lives and that one girl lost an eye in the accident. I mentioned a number of incidents publicly at that gathering, the incidents that had taken place already, and I said that those incidents did not contribute towards the improvement of the security situation and that we have to take the custody of the peace and security in the town in our hands. I also said that I understood various interpretations of the event and that I understood that the relationship between the Serbs and the Croats were slightly impaired as a result of the war that had raged -- started raging in Croatia, because we bordered on Croatia. The only thing between us was the River Sava, the thing that connected us or separated us, whichever way you want to take it. I like to think that the Sava connects us. I also said that somebody in this town, at any costs, wanted to impair the good relationship that existed between the Serbs and the Croats, and I, in that, implied the Croatian Democratic Action Party -- the Democratic Action Party. After that, Mr. Tihic asked the floor. Obviously, he refused to agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Zaric is still talking a bit too fast. On page 70 it was said that someone wanted to impair the good relationships that existed between the Serbs and the Muslims, not Croats. And then that he was referring to the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA. And here it says Serbs and Croats and the Croatian Democratic Action Party. So maybe he could give his answer again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe he can go over that slowly so that it's clear and recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you've heard. You have to slow down a little so that your words can be recorded correctly. What did you say about the relationship between the Croats and Serbs, and Serbs and Muslims, and when you mentioned the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the speed of my speech. I'm trying to discipline myself, but it is very hard for me. I'll try to speak as slowly as possible and help our interpreters. I have stated the following: Although the relationship between the Croats and the Serbs had been impaired because of the war in Croatia, and that atmosphere had a bearing on the overall relationship between the Croats and the Serbs. I did not see the reason why somebody in this town is all the time trying to impair the good relationship between the Serbs and Muslims that had lasted for a long time. I lived in that town from 1969 onwards and I never had any problems with either Croats or Muslims. There were never any serious political or security situations of that sort which all of a sudden appeared on the public scene, and for that reason I pointed to that fact, because the two young men who spoke before me and who took the floor before me, their idea was that as monuments should be erected to the two killed people and that this should be erected next to the monument of the victims of the Second World War, and so on and so forth. Some very unrealistic requests were raised, and my goal was to calm down the atmosphere and to end the meeting on a sober note. My appeal to everybody was to fight for our unity, for all of us to find the strength to overcome that situation and to mourn any young person who dies for nothing, for no reason at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you said that Mr. Tihic took the floor.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tihic took the floor and he made me understand that the Party of Democratic Action was a democratic modern party which fostered plurality of views, that it didn't engage in any hitting below the belt. Obviously this was a political stage and everybody wanted to gain points for themselves and to portray themselves in as good light as possible. My speech and my intentions, however, were very honest and I had all the good intentions when I spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting or that rally, did it in any way contribute to the calming down of the situation that prevailed in Samac? Did it improve the relationship among the ethnic groups in the town or did the segregation continue even after that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I must say that for the first couple of days after that, the situation calmed down a little and the tension subsided somewhat. The burial of these two young men was attended by everybody, by members of all the ethnic groups. For me it was a good sign. It was a sign that people mourned for these two young people, and I thought that this was -- this would contribute to the calming down of the overall situation. Unfortunately, this happened over the two dead bodies. But I thought that it would help. However, after two or three days, the things escalated and went in a very unwanted direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. Do you have any personal knowledge about the launching of a mortar shell on a village in Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. That happened before the Valentine's Day, before the incident in the Valentino Cafe. That was on the 8th of December [as interpreted], 1992, when the paramilitary formations from Hasic village launched 120-millimetre grenade towards Skaric village. That mortar shell fell in a field not far from the Babic and Bogdanovic family's houses. Mr. Makso Simeunovic, this was in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Detachment, but immediately after that, Mr. Simeunovic told me that a team of experts had gone there and carried out an inspection, realised what kind of a mortar shell that was, informed the security service about that, and I know that Mr. Lukac has testified here before this Trial Chamber that they tried to find the perpetrator and they tried fire to that piece of weaponry, however without any success.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, this incident, as far as you said, you said on the 8th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 8th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript was not correct. It entered in the transcript that this happened on the 8th of December, which was wrong. Do you remember the kind of pressures that were put on members of the 4th Detachment who were different ethnic group to leave the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: I must say that this was our daily nightmare. Although we tried very hard to keep as many of us together in the 4th Detachment, and by that I mean people of different ethnic groups. All the while the Party of Democratic Action tried to use different methods to prevent their people from joining us. However, immediately before the outbreak of the war, there were 154 Muslims in the 4th Detachment. There were 44 Croats. There were over 250 Serbs. This shows that we had succeeded in our intentions, but not to be -- not so much as to be able to fully cover our town for defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard testimony before this Trial Chamber about some sorts of pressures. A pamphlet was mentioned before this Trial Chamber. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: This was just one of the forms of pressure. We knew, we were aware of that fact. Mr. Fitozovic also admitted that here. But I, as a very experienced security officer, I realised that an action had been taken. He sent his people to the 4th Detachment to spy on us and to gather intelligence. Another type of action was a pamphlet that, on the 1st of April of 1992, turned up on the tree trunks and on the walls of business premises all over the town. This enemy pamphlet, and that is all I can call it, I can't call it anything else - was worded in such a way as to convey a message to those Muslims who were members of the 4th Detachment, were given a deadline by the 6th of April of 1992 to leave the 4th Detachment or else. They would be treated as traitors and they would be judged by the Muslim people. I happened to have that paper in front of me when I talked to Mr. Tihic when he was arrested, and let me just say that this pamphlet caused a strong embitterment, of the feeling of embitterment. It was presented here as exhibit on several occasions, so I don't want to go back to that exhibit but to use the words, "Chetniks, Chetnik leaders, Chetnik slaughterers," this is something that can be attributed only to Serbs, as something arising from the history, and this time these attributes were given to them. So this pamphlet caused a great deal of dissatisfaction among the members of the 4th Detachment and the general population, I would say, the general population that resided in town at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but on page 74, line -- the second line, it reads in the transcript: "He," referring to Mr. Fitozovic," he sent his people to the 4th Detachment to spy on us." What do you exactly mean by "us"? Is it the 4th Detachment or perhaps an ethnic group? Could you clarify that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that, I'm talking about the people who were given the task by Mr. Fitozovic to be members of the detachment, to attend our meetings and to possibly report from that meetings and to convey certain intentions of ours to Mr. Fitozovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm only asking for your explanation of the word "us." "He sent his people to the 4th Detachment to spy on us." What did you mean by the word "us"? Stick to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the entire 4th Detachment. I did not mean any particular ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And there is just one small correction for the transcript. Two words from the sentence are missing, just to give some meaning to the words. It's on page 74, on line 15: But to use the word Chetniks, Chetnik leaders, Chetnik slaughterers for the Muslims, because Mr. Zaric was referring to the Muslim members of the 4th Detachment. Yes. Because here we don't see that Mr. Zaric is referring to the Muslim members. So when he gives an explanation, "Chetniks, Chetnik leaders, Chetnik slaughterers," this is something that can be attributed only to the Serbs, and he was referring to Muslims who were offended by using such words for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Maybe he can explain that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you have heard what has given rise to confusion. Could you explain to us what you were saying a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: There were perhaps 10 to 15 names on that leaflet, the names of all the people on that leaflet were the names of people of Muslim nationality. And by their names, for example, it would say Fadil Topcagic-Chetnik Vojvoda, Chetnik leader. This is incomprehensible in our Balkan area and in our former Yugoslav area, it's incomprehensible to ascribe such terms to Muslims. These are terms that could only be applied to Serbs or Chetnik slaughterer, butcher, et cetera. These are derogatory terms which were always used to refer to the Serbs. And this is why I'm saying that it is incomprehensible and unacceptable to see terms used to refer to Serbs which had been placed by Muslim names on those leaflets, and these are terms that were used with reference to Serbs throughout history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, let's just clarify one other matter. You said that all these people were of Muslim nationality. Were all the men, all the men on this leaflet, members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were all members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just two small corrections for the transcript. The correct interpretation when said Chetnik Vojvoda, this means -- the exact translation of Vojvoda is duke. It's a title, something like. And there are -- there is also one word missing that Mr. Zaric used two times. He was talking about frustrated history, and here it says on page 76, line 10, there is this word frustrated history. He was using this. And he has very special meaning when he says frustrated history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because here it is recorded to Serbs throughout history. Yes. I don't think we need to go into that. I think we can proceed with the evidence, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened immediately after these leaflets had been distributed? What happened in the town of Samac which contributed to the deterioration of the relations between all the citizens there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, up until that date when the leaflet appeared, we had a meeting in the local commune, the Crisis Staff, and at that meeting naturally we condemned such behaviour and I felt free to speculate on the identity of the person who had decided that such leaflets should be distributed. And on the following day, in the afternoon of the 2nd of April, 1992, there was that notorious incident that has been discussed on several occasions before this Trial Chamber. That was when the reserve policemen of the Samac police station, the Samac public security station, seriously wounded three members who were in civilian clothing at the time, and they were in a vehicle. But these people, these men, were members of the 4th Detachment. Their names were Danilo Vitomir, Mirsad Mesic, who was a butcher, and Nisad Ramusovic, also known as Tota, one of the Ramusovic brothers. And that incident showed that the security situation -- the overall security situation in the town had come to a head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. The answer by Mr. Zaric, on page 77, line 6, refers to the Crisis Staff, and the date he mentioned was the 2nd of April. As far as I know, there was no Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac at that time. Could the witness perhaps clarify the concepts as to dates and time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as the Crisis Staff is concerned, Mr. Zaric has already mentioned it on two occasions in the course of his testimony, but I didn't think it was necessary to ask him about that Crisis Staff, or it was called the coordination body in that local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you tell us what you mean by Crisis Staff in the local commune of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, this Crisis Staff should in fact be distinguished from the Crisis Staff that is the matter of particular attention here. The Crisis Staff in the local commune of Samac commenced its work in the month of February and it existed only within the local commune of Samac. It was represented by representatives of political parties in the town, members of the council of the local commune, from the local commune, and I represented the 4th Detachment. I participated at meetings of that Crisis Staff on behalf of the detachment, of the 4th Detachment. In fact, that was an operative body which met very frequently on the premises of the local commune, in the well-known pensioners' home, and every day or every few days we would discuss the current political and security situation in the town, in the local commune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So this Crisis Staff you mentioned should not be mixed up with the Crisis Staff which was formed at the 15th of April and headed by Dr. Blagoje Simic? There are two different things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will turn to the subject of the Crisis Staff in the local commune later on, so I won't pursue this matter that Mr. Zaric has just addressed, but I will carry on with the subject that we were discussing before the Trial Chamber asked this question about the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that the reserve policemen fired at, were they in a civilian vehicle at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in a civilian vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Since when I found out about the incident I immediately went to the medical centre, I was able to see the three men when the ambulance managed to treat them and send them to hospital in Tuzla and Brcko. They were all wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, were you at the site where this incident occurred? Did you see that passenger vehicle in which Mesic, Ramusovic, and Vitomir were travelling?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I later went to the site and I saw that Lada car at the crossroads. I don't know what the names of the streets are exactly, but it wasn't far from the Molla cafe. It was perhaps 30 metres from the Sava River. The vehicle had been riddled with bullets and there were people who were carrying on an on-site investigation from the SJB, the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the SJB in Samac, --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the public security station in Samac. Jovanovic and Lukac were there. But I have to say that I only had a look at the site. I asked them what the situation was. They were doing their work. I asked Mr. Lukac whether they had found weapons or anything of that kind in the vehicle, and I was told that they didn't find weapons or anything else in that car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find anything out about the perpetrators of that attack on those people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very soon, because we were informed that these -- that two reserve -- we were informed that two reserve policemen had opened fire on these three policemen, Izetbegovic Adis is the name of one of them, he is the son of Izo Izetbegovic, and the other is Safet Srna. They were both members of the reserve police force and they had a tendency to destroy public order before that event, and Srna --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One small intervention. On page 80, line 7, it says two reserve policemen had opened fire on these three policemen, these three persons that were shot were not actually policemen. They were members of the 4th Detachment but civilians at that point. They didn't wear any uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you found out about the perpetrators, did you later have the opportunity of seeing those perpetrators in the town of Samac? Were they the members of the reserve police force in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: After the incident, I immediately informed Mr. Makso Simeunovic about what had happened, and the gentlemen you're talking about, these two policemen, we never saw them again, since they are both active reserve policemen who were members of various ethnic groups in the SJB. We found out that both policemen had been taken by a police car to Croatia immediately after the incident. They never returned. They more or less fled from the site. And when certain measures were requested, we were told that they didn't have access to them, that they weren't in the area of Samac. And according to the intelligence we had, they had crossed over into Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The on-site investigation that was conducted, if I've understood you correctly, you said that this investigation was already being carried out by members of the Samac SJB. Did the security organs of the JNA of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA, or anyone else from the JNA, conduct any sort of on-site investigation into this incident?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, nothing at all. The on-site investigation was carried out by members of the SJB alone. I think that was their professional duty. All the people who were wounded were civilians, and there was absolutely no reason for military security to get involved. And the only thing that interested me when I appeared at the scene and saw the people I had mentioned was what I have already mentioned. I didn't want to get involved in any sort of investigation. That wasn't my task and that wasn't included in my duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who carried out on-site investigations and compiled reports about on-site investigations and prepared documents that concerned all incidents in the municipality of Samac and sabotage in the incidents?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: It was the SJB and the relevant investigations judge, who would go to the site and carry out on-site investigations. I remember that Zeljko Senic was one of the persons who was at the site and carried out an on-site investigation with Mr. Lukac, Savic, and Zoran Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of a single incident, act of sabotage or an incident of some other kind, for which the security from the JNA carried out the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such incident. I don't know of security organs from the 17th Tactical Group carrying out an on-site investigation into sabotage or terrorist act that may have occurred or that occurred during the period that I have been speaking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the police or, rather, the public security service in Bosanski Samac discovered a single perpetrator of an act of sabotage or of some other kind of act during this period?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I'm not familiar with any such information, in spite of the fact that there were numerous incidents and in spite of the fact that this -- these are incidents that occurred in a restricted area. I have to quite simply say that -- well, Mr. Lukac, in my opinion, was one of the most capable officials, as far as investigations occurred in the Doboj region at that time. That was his reputation, and I had a high opinion of him. However, I have to say that unfortunately not a single incident was discovered or attributed to someone who had committed an act of sabotage. And this is a somewhat worrying fact. And until such a difficult situation developed, the perpetrators of various acts and sleight acts, they were soon discovered and legal measures were taken against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, who was the chief of the SJB, the public security station, in Bosanski Samac? In 1991 and for part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: The chief of the SJB was Mr. Vinko Dragicevic. He was there on behalf of the HDZ after the multiparty elections. He had been appointed to that post and he replaced Radovan Antic, who was the former chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vinko Dragicevic is of Croatian nationality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC
utterances.text: Vinko Dragicevic is a Croat. He is a lawyer from the village of Hasici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is now time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Maybe just to assist the interpreters. The question was: Mr. Zaric was the chief of SJB and the answer was: In 1991 and for part of 1992, this was still a question. And then comes the answer the chief of SJB was Vinko Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And then on line 4, that was a question. "Vinko Dragicevic is of Croat nationality?" And then the answer Vinko Dragicevic is a Croat. He was a lawyer from the village of Hasici. And that's the correct order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
